properties.summary: Sinosauropteryx was a small meat-eating dinosaur from northeastern China whose fossils show a fringe of fine filaments along the body. Most scientists see these as simple feather-like coverings and have used tiny pigment structures to suggest a striped tail. A small group of researchers argued in 2007 that the filaments are broken-down skin fibers instead, and Joel Tay of Creation Ministries International makes a similar case. Other researchers replied in 2017 that the fiber idea came from misread features.

views.mainstream: Most paleontologists read the filaments as simple feather-like body covering; pigment-structure (melanosome) studies were used to infer a banded tail and countershading (Zhang et al. 2010; Smithwick et al. 2017).
views.collagen_fiber_view_non_creationist: Lingham-Soliar, Feduccia & Wang (2007, Proc. R. Soc. B) argued the filaments are degraded skin collagen fibres. DOI verified: 10.1098/rspb.2007.0352.
views.reply: Smithwick et al. (2017, Palaeontology) argued the collagen reading came from misidentified features and supported feather homologues.
views.ministry_view: CMI (Joel Tay) presents the collagen reading as evidence the filaments are not feathers (attributed claim only).

properties.related_note: Similar filament finds (e.g., Dilong, Yutyrannus, Beipiaosaurus) are reviewed in Xu & Barrett 2025, Biology Letters (https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2024.0517); not separate pins in this starter pack.
